Guṇabhadra (in the Liang language, "Virtuous Merit") was a native of Central India. In his youth, he studied the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): astronomy, literature, mathematics, medicine, and incantations.

He reached a profound mastery of worldly arts and crafts, including the principles of wind, breath, and the void. Possessing firm resolve and clear intelligence, he specialized in the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) scriptures.
Fearing that the miscellaneous matters of non-Buddhist texts might corrupt the teachings of the Śākya clan, he fled to the Kingdom of Siṃhala and took refuge there.
The Master entered the Way and devoted himself single-mindedly to his studies. He declined the Lesser Vehicle and practiced the Greater; thus, he was known in the world as Mahayana.

The Master wished to test him and ordered him to enter a dark room and retrieve a case of scriptures. He immediately obtained the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. The Master said, "The Great Vehicle has a profound karmic affinity for you.
He then sent a letter to the master's parents, exhorting them to return to the True Dharma, saying: "If you remain solely devoted to external paths..."
"Though you return, it will be of no benefit. If you take refuge in the Triple Gem, then you shall long enjoy the privilege of attending upon me.

The father was moved by these sincere words and consequently abandoned heterodoxy to follow the Right Path. Shortly thereafter, Guṇabhadra provided him with provisions and requested that he travel toward the East.

He then boarded a merchant ship and sailed across the sea. In the spring of the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, he finally arrived at Guangzhou and stayed at Yunfeng Mountain, where he established a monastery named after the mountain.
This was for the sake of his reputation. At that time, the Provincial Governor Che Lang submitted a memorial reporting the matter. Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty dispatched an envoy to welcome him.

He arrived at the capital that winter solstice and was ordered to reside at Zhihuan Temple. He was summoned from afar to the palace to transmit and translate [the scriptures]; the Emperor’s disposition was joyful and cordial, as if they were old acquaintances.
The Emperor held him in great esteem and regarded him as extraordinary. Yan Yanzhi of Langya, a man of vast talent and profound learning, came to his door wearing his official belt.
Consequently, the monastics and laypeople of the capital lined the streets with their carriage canopies touching one another. Prince Yixuan of Pengcheng and Qiao appointed him as his teacher.

The assembly of monks collectively requested that he translate scriptures; thus, at Zhihuan Temple, he gathered various monks specializing in the study of meaning, and first translated the *Saṃyuktāgama* in five fascicles.
In ten fascicles. Furthermore, at Dongan Temple, he produced the *Dharmabherī-sūtra* in two fascicles and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in two fascicles.
He also produced the *Paramārtha-pañcalakṣaṇa-uddāna* in one fascicle. Later, at Zhouyang County, he translated the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in one fascicle.
Furthermore, at Daochang Temple, he produced the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* in four fascicles and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in four fascicles, with over seven hundred monks in attendance.
The person was Baoyun, who acted as the oral translator while Huiquan took up the brush. They skillfully analyzed the text and its meaning, achieving a profound understanding.

From the twenty-third year of the Yuanjia era onward, when Prince Xiao Qiao was stationed in Jingzhou, he invited [Baoyun] to accompany him. There they rested at Xin Temple and further established a main hall and chambers.
Thereupon, within the monastery, he produced one scroll of the *Aśoka-rāja-sūtra*, one scroll of the *Aṣṭamaṅgala-sūtra*,
four scrolls of the *Pūrvāparahetu-phala-sūtra*, one scroll of the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha*, and one scroll of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*— in total, thirteen works comprising seventy-three scrolls.
Prince Qiao wished to invite him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and other scriptures, but Guṇabhadra reflected that he was not yet proficient in the Chinese language.
Gu spoke with difficulty for many days, feeling ashamed and distressed. He immediately performed prostrations and repentance day and night, praying for a response from the unseen realm.
Consequently, he dreamed of a person dressed in white, holding a sword and carrying a human head, who came before him and asked, "Why are you grieving?

Gu fully explained the matter to him. The figure replied, "It does not hurt," and then suddenly vanished. Gu awoke with his mind filled with joy. When he rose the next morning, he was able to fully comprehend all the points of doctrine discussed.
In the Han language, he then began his exposition. The disciple Fayong served as the translator, while Sengnian acted as the *dougang* (chief lecturer).

He asked, "Master, how do you observe the military array of my disciples? He replied, "It is like a mass of ink."

With single-minded devotion, he invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara, grasped a *qióngzhú* staff in his hand, and threw himself into the river. The water reached only up to his knees, yet he prodded the water with his staff.
The water was deep and the current swift. He saw a young boy who had followed after him; he reached out his hand and pulled the boy along.
Looking back, he said to the boy, "How can you, a mere child, ferry me across? In the blink of an eye, he realized they had already walked some ten paces and had reached the shore.

He immediately removed his outer robe (*nāṃśuka*) and wished to welcome the youth; looking around, however, he could not see him. His hair stood on end all over his body, and only then did he realize it was due to supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

The Emperor looked at him and, entrusting him with his inquiries, said, "I have long harbored this hope; only now do we meet. Guṇabhadra replied, "Since my consciousness has been defiled by delusion, I am but ashes and dust.
That I may now have the honor of your audience is a profound favor bestowed upon me. The Emperor then asked, "Whom do you designate as the thief?"
The response was: "Those who have left the household life do not participate in military affairs. However, Zhang Chang, Zong Lingxiu, and others all coerced me to clarify [the matter].

On that day, he issued an edict for him to reside in the Rear Hall, providing robes and offerings, and granting him attendants and vehicles. Previously, Guṇabhadra had been at Jingzhou.
He remained at the court for ten years. Whenever he corresponded with foreign kings, he recorded every letter without exception.

When the military was defeated and his records were examined, not a single word concerning military affairs could be found. Emperor Xiaowu recognized that his meticulousness was merely a pretext and treated him with even greater courtesy.

Later, during a casual conversation, the Emperor jokingly asked, "Do you think of the Chancellor? He replied, "Having received his provisions for ten years, how could I forget his virtue? Now, following Your Majesty..."
He knelt and requested, "I pray that you will burn incense for the Chancellor for three years. The Emperor’s countenance moved with sorrowful emotion; moved by the request, he granted it.

When Zhongxing Temple was completed, an imperial decree ordered him to move there and provided him with three rooms. Later, during a banquet at the Eastern Palace where princes and dukes had all assembled, the Emperor received Guṇabhadra by imperial command.
At that time, he had not yet shaved his head, and his hair was white and brilliant. Emperor Xiaowu gazed at him from afar.

The Emperor turned to the Minister Xie Zhuang and said, "Mahāyāna is intelligent and possesses keen understanding; however, his years have reached their end. Let me test him; he will surely grasp the intent of my words.

For forty years, he had enjoyed the profound favor of imperial grace, yet his grief was boundless, as if he were biting on a clod of earth. However, at seventy years of age, he was frail with illness, and death was his only certainty.

The Emperor, admiring his wit and eloquence, issued an edict for him to sit near the imperial throne; the entire court frequently turned their eyes toward him. Later, he established a monastery west of the Phoenix Tower in the borders of Moling.
Every time it reached midnight, there would be someone knocking at the door and calling out, yet when they looked, no person was to be seen. This happened repeatedly among the assembly.
He repeatedly had distressing dreams. Guṇabhadra burned incense and recited a mantra, saying: "You have resided here due to past affinities.

Now that I am establishing a monastery, practicing the Way, and performing repentance, you who dwell here shall serve as the guardian deities of this temple. If you cannot remain, go wherever you find peace.
Subsequently, more than ten monastics and laypeople all dreamed on the same night that thousands of ghosts and spirits were all carrying their belongings and moving away.
He departed, and the community of the monastery was subsequently at peace. In the seventh year of the Daming era, a severe drought occurred throughout the land.
Prayers were offered to the mountains and rivers for many days without result. Emperor Xiaowu requested that he be allowed to pray for rain, stipulating that there must be a response;

he added that if it proved ineffective, they need not meet again. Guṇabhadra replied: "I rely upon the Triple Gem; by the majesty of Your Majesty’s heavenly authority, the rain will surely descend. If it is not obtained, I shall not [return]."
He saw it again. He immediately went to the Fishing Platform at the Northern Lake, where he burned incense and offered prayers.

Abstaining from food and drink, he silently recited the sutras and secretly added secret mantras. At the hour of *bhu* the following day, clouds rose in the northwest like a carriage canopy as the sun hung low over the mulberry trees.

The wind shook and the clouds gathered; that very day, rain fell. The next morning, the high officials entered to offer congratulations, and by imperial decree, he was granted an audience and comforted.
Alms and offerings followed one after another. Since his youth, Bhadra had maintained a vegetarian diet for his entire life and always carried an incense burner, never letting it leave his hand.
Every time he finished eating, he would invariably share his food; birds would flock to his hands to take the food. This continued until the reign of Emperor Ming, when he received ritual offerings.

His illness grew increasingly severe. On the first day of the first month of the fourth year of the Taishi era, he felt his body was unwell and took leave of Emperor Ming and the high officials in advance.
On the day of his passing, as he stood gazing at the clouds, he beheld celestial flowers and sacred images. At the hour of Youzhong, he passed away.

He was seventy-five years old at his death. Emperor Ming felt profound grief and sorrow for him, providing generous consolations and funeral subsidies. The high officials assembled for the funeral, and all honors were fully bestowed upon him.
Subsequently, there arrived Guṇavidi, a man from Central India, who was intelligent, perceptive, and possessed a keen memory.

He could recite over one hundred thousand words of scripture and was also proficient in the arts of *yīnyáng* and spiritual techniques. He came to China during the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty and resided at Bisha Temple.
He left the monastery. In the tenth year of the Yongming era, he translated the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* and the *Sūtra of the Elder Kiṃśuka*.
He also founded Zhengguan Monastery (and so forth).

Dao’an’s original surname was Wei. All the records of the various pseudo-Qin states state that he was a native of Fuliu in Changshan.
While still an infant, his family was beset by worldly calamities; he was raised by his maternal uncle, the Kong family. At the age of seven, he already understood the sounds of the characters.

He devoted himself to reading; he had already attained a partial mastery of the textual meanings of the Five Classics. By the time he reached the age for committing his studies to memory, he developed a deep inclination toward the Buddhist Way.
At eighteen, he left the household life. He was exceptionally intelligent and discerning, and he established a separate meditation hall for his residence.
There, in a place of tranquil excellence, bamboos stood in rows and flowering medicinal herbs were spread everywhere; it was named Tanxi Temple. Fu Jian dispatched an envoy to present foreign gold.
There was one standing image, seven chi in height; one seated image made of gold; one Maitreya image adorned with pearls;

and one each of images embroidered with golden thread and woven images. Whenever a lecture hall was established, he would vigorously promote the teachings, providing a guiding framework that expanded the profound essence of the Way.
With his enlightened vision and rational thought, those who cherished the Dao arrived carrying their books. At that time, he was fifty years of age.

Suddenly, a strange monk arrived seeking lodging. His appearance was haggard and unkempt, and his robes were soiled and worn. Because the rooms were cramped, he was accommodated in the lecture hall. At midnight, someone rose and saw that the doors of the lecture hall were not open, yet the monk had leaped out through the window. The *vina* (chant leader) reported this to Dao’an; Dao’an called him in for conversation and asked, "For what purpose have you come here? I hope you will tell me the truth. He replied: [The monk said: "I am from the kingdom of Kucha. My name is Dharmakṣema. I have heard that the Great Master Dao’an has attained the Way, and I have come from afar to pay my respects. However, I fear that the Master’s disciples may be arrogant and haughty, and thus I did not dare to announce myself. Therefore, I have stayed hidden in the wilderness for some time. Now, having heard that the Master is about to preach the Dharma, I have come to listen. But I am afraid that the Master’s disciples might see me and drive me away. Thus, I have remained concealed within the lecture hall. I did not wish to trouble the Master with my presence, nor did I wish to cause alarm among the assembly. That is why I leaped out through the window. Dao’an said, "You are truly a man of great virtue. You have come from afar to seek the Dharma. Please stay here and do not leave. He then provided him with food and clothing, and treated him with the utmost respect. From that time on, the monk lived there, and Dao’an relied upon him to translate the scriptures. This was the beginning of the transmission of the *Mahāyāna* teachings in China. It is said that the monk was none other than the Bodhisattva Maitreya. When Dao’an first met him, he had already been in China for over thirty years. He was more than eighty years old when he passed away. His remains were enshrined at Mount Lu. Later generations erected a stupa for him at the site where he died. It is said that whenever the wind blows through the valley, one can still hear the sound of his chanting. Those who hear it feel as though they are in the presence of the Buddha. This is the reason why the world calls him the "Bodhisattva of the Western Regions" (*Xiyu Pusa*). His legacy continues to this day. Those who study the Dharma should take him as their model. One must never harbor thoughts of pride or arrogance. Only by practicing humility and reverence can one receive the guidance of the sages. This is the true path to attaining liberation. Tanyi’s original surname was Yao. He was born in the territory of the Qiang people. At the age of sixteen, he took Dao’an as his teacher and became proficient in the Mahāyāna teachings.

Kumārajīva was even more refined in his mastery of the Tripiṭaka; his talent and insight were brilliant and outstanding. Although he did not surpass Dao’an, his integrity and ascetic practice were pure and rigorous, such that none among his disciples could rival him.
During the Jin dynasty, the Grand Governor of Changsha, who held a prominent residence in Jingzhou, admired Dao’an’s character and virtue and wished to travel far to welcome and invite him.

He offered his own residence to be converted into a monastery and requested Dao’an to seek out a monk to serve as its abbot. Dao’an looked back and said to Huìyì: "The gentry and commoners of Jing and Chu..."
When he first desired to return to his ancestral home and bring its excellence to fruition, who else could it have been but you? As you were traveling, you assisted Zhiqing as he journeyed south;

upon arriving, you oversaw the construction, completing the work in one year. It was named Changsha Temple. Later, while traveling through the Gaibu region, you encountered the Regional Inspector Mao Qu, who held you in high esteem from their very first meeting.
He immediately provided you with a thousand *hu* of rice and prepared a midday meal for you. Within that rice, you found a single grain of millet.
He immediately selected and ate the first portion. Xu sighed and said, "Could this śramaṇa truly be one who rejects the offerings of men?

He then bestowed upon him generous gifts and soon returned to Jingzhou. When the rebel Qiu entered the territory and plundered the region south of the Han River, the entire jurisdiction of Jiangling was affected.
Huiyi also built Dong Temple at Shangming. Later, he returned to Changsha Temple, where he further established Kaiyou Temple and constructed a great stupa along with a sixteen-foot golden image.
As no śarīra had yet been obtained, he prayed for many years until they were suddenly found.
He immediately gathered five hundred monks and nuns, burned incense, and chanted praises; he requested a bowl of water to float the śarīra.
The śarīra turned to the right, emitting five-colored light that was so clear and penetrating it filled the entire room.
He subsequently went to Mount Yiling (also known as Mount Kuoting in the *Shanhai jing*) to fell timber; atop this mountain was a dark cavern that secretly connected to Baoshan in Wu.
As the mountain was both divine and extraordinary, travelers feared it. The Master said: "Huan Xuan heard there were white pheasants and rabbits on the mountain, and thus went there."
He searched for it, losing his way for several days. Although the boat appeared very close, he could not reach it. On the following day, he encountered dozens of white snakes blocking the path.
He preached the Dharma to them, whereupon the snakes cleared the way. That night, he had a dream in which they said: "These woods are what we cherish."
Once the Buddha stūpa was under construction, he provided the necessary materials; however, he strictly forbade his subordinates from taking anything by unlawful means.

All the laborers were hired on a temporary basis, so that no one would have cause for theft. Upon reaching Jiangling, when the scaffolding was already erected but the timber had not yet been removed, it was seized by soldiers.

He then demolished the previous small stūpa and established a larger one in its place. Furthermore, he cast a sixteen-foot golden image. Having previously entered into an agreement with two artisans...
A great assembly was convened; may there be no obstacles or hindrances. Upon hearing this, the fourfold assembly rejoiced and followed with delight.

The copper obtained from the *hu* [vessel] was more than sufficient for all expenses; what remained was used to further construct sacred ritual implements: an incense burner seven feet high, and vestments of brocade to clothe the divine image.
Disciples gathered there in great numbers, and they often lamented that while the monastery was sufficient for the assembly of monks, the sacred images were still too few.

They had heard that King Aśoka had produced many Buddha images and distributed them according to circumstances, yet none had ever reached this place. "Is it not," they wondered, "that our sincerity has not yet reached him?
Thereupon, they redoubled their earnest devotion. On the night of the eighth day of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Yonghe era, an image suddenly appeared in the city.
In the north, the light from his body illuminated the night as brightly as the dawn, causing the entire continent to stir with awe.

People gathered from near and far. At that time, one hundred men were dispatched by Baima Temple to welcome him; though they exerted all their strength, they could not move him. Daoyi said, "This must be a statue of King Aśoka;
it is destined for Changsha Temple and cannot be shifted by brute force. Everyone agreed, saying, "Please test this; it will surely be proven effective. Daoyi then prostrated himself.

He paid his respects. He commanded five of his disciples to lift and carry it; they rose up with a light, soaring motion. The fourfold assembly was struck with awe and submission, and asked for the reason behind this.
Daoyi smiled and said, "In the past, I made a sincere vow. Based on my reasoning, I knew it would come to pass after that.
Later, the Kasmirian meditation master Saṃghananda came down from Shu to enter the temple and prostrate. He remarked, "This is a foreign image," and proceeded to search for its inscriptions.

Regarding the "Buddha’s Radiance" (Foguang): there was indeed a manuscript in Hu script, which read, "Created by King Aśoka. [The author] was eighty-two years old when he passed away at Zhongyi Temple (and so forth).

While residing at Waguan Temple, Wang Dao and Kong Fu both sought his counsel and formed a bond of mutual understanding. Later, he lived on Baoshan in Shining.
His retinue consisted of more than forty people, all of whom were eminent Daoist masters who had grasped the profound mysteries; they served him without fail throughout the four seasons.

In the second year of the Xuanan era, he contracted a severe illness that could not be cured by acupuncture or moxibustion. He focused his mind exclusively on the recitation of the name of Avalokiteśvara. After some time, he suddenly dreamed.
A śramaṇa extracted his intestines and stomach, removed all impurities and ailments, washed them with clear water, and returned them to their place within his body.

Upon waking, he felt a sudden and complete recovery. When Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty ascended the throne, he invited him to the capital because of his renowned virtue and constantly sought his counsel as a teacher.
The Emperor provided him with exceptionally generous support. At the age of seventy-four, he passed away in the fifth year of the Taiyuan era. The Emperor [bestowed] ten coins...

Wan purchased Xinting Hill to serve as his burial site and erected a three-story stupa. At that time, there were also the monks Shi Pusui and Shi Huijian, who resided at Shengzhong Monastery in Linhai;

Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Ten:

The Venerable’s name was Sengxing; his original surname was Zhi. He was a native of Shanyin, Kuaiji. At the age of thirteen, he left the household life as a disciple of Dharma Master Ji and resided at Chengbang Temple.
He would often say: "The Way of the Immortals ultimately involves decline and fall; [only] the Profound and the Confucian..."
In terms of teaching that cannot transcend the mundane world, refining and polishing the mind and spirit, and opening up wisdom and enlightenment, none surpasses that of the Śākya clan.

Thus, [the Master] opened the scriptures to inquire about the Way; his dignified deportment was grandly complete, and he constantly cherished every moment. His fellow student, the Venerable Senglei, enjoyed great renown throughout the Eastern Lands.

Together with the Venerable [Dao]hui—who served as the foundation for [the Master’s] influence—they jointly propagated the supreme teaching. Senglei was a native of Shanyin; his physical bearing and temperament were expansive.
Tai’s character was refined and far-reaching. Sengji often remarked, "Those who can truly enhance and benefit social customs are none other than Xing and Kui.
Because the world was noisy and distracting, the Upādhyāya moved his residence to Fahua Temple; from then on, except for matters concerning the Dharma, he did not set foot below the mountain.

Thereupon, he propagated the Dharma teachings and provided instruction and guidance. The assembly of monks was orderly, and through his constant transformation of them, they were filled with joy. They kept the Western Land in mind, vowing to be reborn in Sukhāvatī.
At the age of fifty-nine, he passed away in the eleventh year of the Yongming era. He also had a fellow student named Huītong, who was his junior.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume XI:

Fayu (the separate biography calls him Tanyu; another record calls him Daoyu). He was a man of unknown origins. From his youth, he was resolute and noble in spirit, and he cultivated and sought [the Dharma].
He lived in seclusion. When the wife of a wealthy neighbor sought to marry him, and the Prefect summoned him to serve as an official, he declined both.
He devoted himself exclusively to the Great Dharma, taking Shi Dao’an as his teacher. Having bathed in the profound transformation of the teachings, he consulted on matters of obscure principle.

He held to his practice with sincere devotion, and his observance of the prohibitions was never lax. [Dao’an] bestowed upon him the affection of rubbing the crown of his head and granted him the praise of one who inspires progress. Thereupon, he drew the curtain to study in private.
Fayye was extensively versed in the profound sutras. Chen Di and Ruan Bao, the Governors of Yiyang, heard of his reputation and admired him;

they sent letters to establish friendly relations, and messengers traveled back and forth. Consequently, he received offerings and gifts. In the second year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the temple was located within the city walls of Xiangyang.
Together with Tanwei, Tanyi, Yuanhui, and others, he gathered disciples below at Jiangling and Changsha. There, the wheel of the Dharma was set in motion, and students flocked there like clouds;
the assembly of those receiving instruction regularly numbered four hundred. Once, a monk drank wine in the monastery and foolishly burned incense at night;
although he encountered punishment, he was not expelled. When Dao’an heard of this, he sealed a plum pit inside a bamboo tube, inscribed it with his own hand, and sent it [to the offender].

Upon encountering [the monk] Kāi-fēng, he saw the staff and immediately said, "This is due to a monk who drinks alcohol. I have failed to diligently train the assembly, thereby causing you to be far removed from my concern.

He then ordered the *vina* (chant leader) to strike the *qing* (bell) to assemble the congregation. With the staff held in a tube, he measured it against the incense burner. After the incense offering was completed, [he struck the bell].

Before emerging from the assembly, he manifested a transformation toward the staff-tube (*zhūng*). Having completed the transformation, he prostrated himself on the ground. He commanded the *karmadāna* to strike him three times with the staff;

as the staff was placed back inside the tube, he rose and again acted out weeping and sobbing. At that time, among the monastics and laypeople within the borders, there were none who did not sigh in lamentation.
Subsequently, he wrote a letter to Huiyuan, saying: "I am unable to lead the assembly. Although the Upādhyāya is separated from me by distant lands, he still extends his concern to me from afar."
"My transgressions are profound. At the age of sixty-one, he passed away in Jiangling (etc.). In the twelfth volume of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Ming seng zhuan*), regarding Daoheng:

The scholar Zhang Zhong saw him and said, "This child possesses the principles of both the Dragon and the Sun. If he serves in office, his rank shall reach that of a high minister;

After his mother’s death, he became renowned for his filial piety. His family circumstances were clear and poor; remaining steadfast in poverty and maintaining careful conduct, he studied and recited scriptures by hand, selling them to provide for his mother’s support until the completion of his mourning period.
Together with his fellow student Daobiao, both attained great renown. When Master Kumārajīva entered the realm, they both participated in the detailed examination and translation of texts.
Emperor Yao Xing held them in high esteem and regard, remarking that they possessed the talent to govern a state. By imperial decree, the titles of *Heng* and *Biao* were conferred upon them.
[Regarding] the Dharma robes, the Emperor issued an edict, saying: "You all embody leisure and delight in the Way, having taken the Dharma-gate to heart. Your pure conduct is truly praiseworthy.

I even comforted Lu Shuai in a butcher’s stall; how much more so for you gentlemen, who have served me loyally and know my history. My words are now exhausted:

each of you possesses the ability to manage affairs of state, yet you remain hidden in a realm of solitary self-cultivation. Is this truly my ultimate sincerity in seeking talent, or your profound intent in promoting transformation?
As the ancients said: "The state possesses a fine steed, yet does not mount it; instead, it wanders aimlessly in search of another. This is precisely the case here.
...so it is said (and so forth). The thirteenth discourse in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:
Question: Regarding the gradual realization of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) by the three vehicles, the sutra says: "The three vehicles equally awaken to the true mark," yet [they attain...]

The Way is the true mark (*dharmatā*). Is there a threefold principle? Does one attain the three fruits by awakening to the three? The true mark is simply emptiness; how could it have a threefold nature?
If the principle of the true mark is one, then by awakening to this one, how can there be three fruits? If one awakens to the one, it should not result in three. Answer:
The true mark is such that not even a single thing can be apprehended, yet there are three. This is because practitioners who engage with conditions awaken [to them].

Emptiness has degrees of depth; it is categorized as threefold based on the practitioner. Question: If the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is such that not a single thing can be apprehended, then upon awakening to it, the principle is exhausted.
If one does not awaken to it, one is like someone facing a wall. Why, then, should there be differences of depth?

Why is it said that there are three [levels] based on the practitioner? Answer: If a practitioner awakens to the fact that the true mark is markless (*animitta*), they must first recognize its marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and only then...

Realizing its lack of characteristics (*animitta*), by what could one define the characteristic of consciousness? It is like the characteristic of birth and death, which arises through the twelve links of dependent origination.
Only the Tathāgata thoroughly perceives the beginning and end of these causes and conditions; he realizes that the definitive characteristic of birth and death is ultimately unattainable.

Thus, this characteristic of consciousness is itself without characteristic. Therefore, it is called the supreme realization of the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). When a Bodhisattva contemplates birth and death...

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination, they perceive only its end but do not recognize its beginning. Although they realize that appearances are not [inherently] real, they do not recognize the beginning of these causes and conditions;

therefore, they are said to be those who have awakened to the midst of true reality (*dharmatā*). Those of the Two Vehicles merely contemplate the phenomena of birth and death as existing through dependent origination;
although they awaken to the fact that appearances are not [inherently] real, they do not become attached to birth and death.
Yet, they understand the beginning and end of the conditions of consciousness; therefore, it is said that awakening to the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is in reality non-dual.

Depending on the practitioner, there is the illumination of light and darkness; by contemplating those various conditions as being either exhausted or inexhaustible, there arise the distinctions of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) within the true mark.
Question: Since both Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles do not exhaustively investigate the beginning of conditions, why is this distinction made?
[Question: How can it be said that one attains the Way by awakening to the true nature (*dharmatā*)? [Answer:

Although Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles do not penetrate the beginning and end of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they understand that birth and death exist through causes and conditions.

They know that the fixed characteristics (*niyata-lakṣaṇa*) of birth and death cannot be apprehended; therefore, they are able to remain unstained by birth and death, transcend the Three Realms, and attain the Way (and so forth).
Furthermore, he asked the one who speaks of the non-existent self: "The sutras state that the false views of the heterodox regarding the self are called 'perverse and inverted.
Now you clarify that Buddha-nature is itself the self, which is called 'right view. Why is it that the heterodox are considered perverse, while Buddha-nature is considered right?
He replied: "The heterodox falsely perceive a self; they take what is impermanent to be permanent. How could this not be perverse? As for the Buddha-dharma..."

Taking ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) as the Buddha-nature, and taking the Buddha as the true self (*ātman*), which is eternally abiding and unchanging—how could this not be the correct [view]?
Question: For what reason is the Buddha-nature called "self"? Answer:
The reason the Buddha-nature is called "self" is that all sentient beings possess the true nature for attaining Buddhahood, a nature that is eternally present; it is nothing other than one's own.

Because it is that which is cherished, it is called the "self" (*ātman*). Question: If the heterodox outsiders falsely perceive a divine self and consider this to be a perverse inversion, it is not yet known whether sentient beings possess a self or do not possess a self. If there is no self, one fears that practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) would be in vain;
who then would receive the retribution for cultivating goodness or committing evil? Answer: Although sentient beings lack a permanent, abiding self, yet...
There exists the mind of good and evil. This mind of good and evil is the sovereign of all practices (*caryā*).
Heaven and hell take this mind as their foundation; the continuity of cause and effect arises from it. Therefore, it is eternal yet non-existent; it ceases yet is never severed.
This is what is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Question: Although the impermanent spirit possesses a mind of good and evil, [regarding] this mind of good and evil—

The mind does not abide for even a single thought-moment. Since the mind that creates good or evil ceases of its own accord once it encounters its object, the future mind is not the master that created the good or evil.
How can one cause the future mind to arbitrarily receive the retribution of the past? This would be like person A suffering calamity on behalf of person B;
how utterly absurd such a judgment from the dark offices of the underworld would be! Answer: As for the objection regarding the future mind—
The mind does not create the karma of past good or evil deeds; how then could one perversely receive the retribution for such past deeds?
This third "later objection" may be called a brilliant and extraordinary proclamation. Indeed, the way of karmic retribution is inconceivable;

even a Bodhisattva of the Tenth Stage can only approximate it, so how could it be something that ordinary people or beginners in their studies could disrupt? Furthermore, one must rely on the literal words and phrases and avoid [arbitrary] interpretations.
This is what is being discussed. The Sūtra says: "Rebirth in the five destinies has the mind as its basis. That which is impermanent is the mind; it shifts constantly from moment to moment.
There is a distinction between the past and the present within me. The preceding mind does not wait for the subsequent mind, yet the subsequent mind exists because of the preceding one."

Through this, birth and death are infinite; through this, karmic retribution is unceasing. As the sutra says: "The seeds of grain from the beginning of the kalpa can produce future grain in infinite succession.
The spirit does not perish, and the mind has no causeless origin. By inferring from grain, one is fully able to understand humanity.

Knowing this, one is sufficiently enlightened to realize there is no soul (ātman). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All dharmas fundamentally arise from causes and conditions; they are empty and without a master.
Is not the meaning of being "without a master" a clear proof that there is no soul?
The Fifteenth Biography of an Eminent Monk:

Jue Shi was a native of Jingzhao. He entered the monastic order at the age of twelve. He was profoundly faithful in his practice and free from worldly desires. He regarded the glory and profit of the world as if they were floating clouds.

He studied the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and established the doctrine of the Two Truths based on the principle that conventional designations are not empty.

He established this as his primary tenet. In scholarly debate, Qingbian was renowned alongside Huijing. His lofty discourse on the profound and transcendent, which accorded with the mind through principle, surpassed that of Shanglue.
Having traveled to Pengcheng in his youth, he later came to the capital region and stayed at Changle Monastery. During the Taishi era, he was widely versed in the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras;

although he did not physically hold a scroll in hand, his contemplation penetrated the most subtle and minute points. There were no doubts regarding the firm rocks or difficulties that he could not resolve.

His ice-like [stiffness] was melted away. He was diligent and courageous, applying himself with energy in all three karmas. When his disciple Sengyao committed a minor transgression regarding wine, he admonished him, saying:
"To indulge one's passions and become negligent, to drink wine to intoxication and eat to satiety—these are all axes that strike at one's character. Do not do such things, even in the cold."
How much more so for those who have stilled their minds; if they can repent earnestly according to the Vinaya, he will grant them a special reprieve for one transgression.

If they do not do so, it is best that they depart far away. Thereupon, his disciples became solemn, and none failed to tremble with awe. The fourfold assembly revered and looked up to him, while people from afar admired his righteousness.
Fifty-nine years of spring and autumn (etc.).
*Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Volume 16:
Tánbǐn. His original surname was Sū; he was a native of Nányáng (Wáng Jīn states he was a native of Jīngzhào). He left home at the age of ten or so and attended upon a śramaṇa...
Dharma Master Hui was his disciple. Suffering from a foot ailment, he did not dare descend to the capital.

In the second year of the Yuanjia era, he went to Jiangling and stayed at Xin Temple, where he partook in lectures on the sutras and śāstras while concurrently practicing dhyāna and the Vinaya. He often struggled with profound contemplation, yet his mind could not fully grasp it.
Later, at Silayer Temple, after finishing his midday meal, he ascended the Prajñā Terrace; becoming weary from reading the scriptures, he lay down to rest and dreamed of one—
A man appeared, his complexion white as silver and his physical marks distinct and clear; he resembled Maitreya.

Raising his hand, he touched [Huiyuan’s] crown and said, "Good son, the doubts you harbor have already been fully resolved within the various treatises and scriptures. Go forth to see for yourself. Upon waking, he was filled with joy.

He subsequently traveled to the capital, where he encountered the Vinaya Master Sengye lecturing on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) in Wu. He immediately went there to listen to the teachings. Thus it was.
He eventually returned to the capital. Following Dharma Master Jinglin at Duobao Monastery, he recited the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and resolved his doubts.
There, he met Yanzhi of Langye at a lecture hall; Yanzhi remarked to Baoyu, the abbot of Duobao Monastery, "This barbarian monk shall become a great vessel.
Later, he went to Xiaoshan in Wuxing to listen to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* from Fayao. He also followed [Dharma Master] Fa... at Nanlin.
Fayye received the *Huayan zaxin* (Avataṃsaka-saṃcaya-hṛdaya) and ate without seeking satiety; he was diligent without complaining of fatigue.
He would read the sūtras by moonlight and did not attend communal feasts. Fayye asked him, "The offerings from the feast are sufficient to purchase oil; for what reason do you not attend? He replied:

When the body moves, the spirit grows weary; when the spirit is weary, one’s deliberations cannot be focused. Without focused deliberation, even study will be without merit. Tánjì was a native of Hé-dōng.
He left home to become a monk at the age of thirteen and became a disciple of Dǎofǎshī. He resided at Dōngsì on Bāgōng Mountain in Shòuyáng.

From his youth, he possessed a dignified bearing, being vast and profound in character. His deportment was upright and solemn, and his intellectual acuity was comprehensive and penetrating. He studied...
He composed the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*. Day and night he continued his work, never resting in peaceful sleep.

He delighted himself in lofty discourse and far-reaching debates, excelling in elegant speech, witty banter, and skillful repartee. Acting as his own master, he received others with an open mind; every movement and action was marked by profound discernment.
He upheld the true Dharma and revealed what had not been heard before. By the time he reached the age of thirty, his reputation had spread throughout the four seas.
When the Son of Heaven heard of his reputation, he invited him to the capital. In the second year of the Daming era of the Song dynasty, he crossed the Yangtze River and resided at Zhongxing Temple.

As the Wheel of Dharma moved forth, the sweet dew of his teachings sprinkled upon the land; scholars from all quarters, though following different paths, arrived together to find their principles satisfied the hearts of the people.

Both monastics and laypeople sighed in admiration. He composed the *Treatise on the Seven Sects*, the first of which established the fundamental tenet: "The Tathāgata appeared in the world because of the primordial..."

There is no Buddhist teaching [that contradicts this]. Therefore, the profound Vaipulya sutras all clearly elucidate that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally non-existent. The discourse on fundamental non-existence has its origins in antiquity.
Why is this so? Before the mysterious creation, there was only vast emptiness; it was only when the primal qi (*yuanqi*) began its transformative evolution that [the world emerged].
Thus, the multitude of forms receive their shapes. Although these forms rely upon transformation (*hua*), the root of that transformative power emerges from spontaneity (*ziran*).
Spontaneity is simply as it is; how could there be an agent who creates it? From this perspective, there is nothing prior to primordial transformation, nor is emptiness the beginning of all forms;
therefore, it is called "Original Non-being" (*benwu*). This does not mean that within a void or gaping abyss, the myriad existents can be produced. Indeed, [End of excerpt]
That which humans are hindered by is hindered by that which has not yet come to be. If one dwells in the mind upon fundamental non-existence, then these burdens will be cleared away.
That "honoring the root can bring rest to the branches" refers precisely to this (and so forth).

Now, ritual and law (*li-fa*) are the earnest teachings of external classics; the precepts and regulations (*jie-lü*) are the supreme models of internal sages.

They block the sprouting of profit and desire and sever the path of depravity and madness, causing the three obstructions and five hindrances to return together to the site of enlightenment (*dao-chang*), while those who drift in evasion or are frivolous and thin-skulled [are brought to reform].

They all attained salvation during the Ren-shou era. Is this not because his compassion was vast and his divine transformations were boundless? Since the Perfectly Awakened One, the Sugata, Kāśyapa compiled the Vinaya into eighty recitations (*bhāṣitas*). "Recitation" means that it should be constantly chanted and maintained. However, as the subtle words gradually drifted apart and the great meanings became contradictory, he eventually took the *Bhikṣu-vibhaṅga* from the *Mātṛkā-piṭaka* and abridged it into the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. *Bāzǔfúló* (婆麤富羅) is the name of the place where the text was composed. It is located in the country of Aparāntaka, in the western regions. This region is the border of the West; its climate is cold and harsh, and its people are fierce and violent. Because of these conditions, they do not cultivate the Way. Furthermore, the land is distant and difficult to reach, so the sages did not transmit their teachings there. Consequently, the Dharma has not spread there. For this reason, the *Vinaya* was not translated [into Chinese] at that time. Later, during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Guṇavarman arrived in the capital. He brought with him the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, which he had obtained from the Western Regions. [Hui]yong struck the horse with his *śikṣā* (monk’s staff), causing the horse to bolt backward and throw its rider to the ground. The camp commander lay prostrate and could not rise immediately; the horse then bolted off into the grass.
The next morning, the commander entered the mountain to offer an apology, claiming that Master Yong had employed supernatural power. Yong said, "I am but a poor monk..."

Tiyun drank wine, yet [Dao]chu never found it strange. Because he habitually struck his monk’s staff, he eventually reached this state. [Tiyun] said, "If this is indeed a change for the better, it must be that the deities of the precepts are protecting me.
Yong was by nature humble and reverent, and practiced asceticism with diligence; even when afflicted by illness, he never failed to maintain his long-term fasts.
He died at the age of eighty-three in the fifth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty (380 CE). (And so forth.)

Huizheng, also known as Tanjie, was originally surnamed Zhuo and was a native of Nanyang. He was the younger brother of Quan, who served as the Minister of External Military Affairs and the Magistrate of Laiyang during the Jin dynasty.

From childhood, his family was so poor that he had no clothes to wear and could not follow teachers or friends. Carrying firewood and warming himself by the flames, he would read and study the Six Classics.
Later, hearing that Yu Fadao was lecturing on the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, he borrowed clothes to attend the lectures. He told his elder brother: [text continues]

He first realized that Confucianism was shallow and mundane, while Daoism was vast and empty; he could no longer exert himself within the secular realm, desiring instead to liberate himself beyond the world of men.
Huiqian said, "Truly, each person has their own mind, but how can one achieve solitary perfection of their will alone? At the age of nineteen, he joined Shi Dao'an as a fellow student.
Dao'an treated him as a close disciple, and they shared a profound mutual understanding and respect. He traveled to various regions to seek further instruction for several years.
In the midst of this, he suddenly inquired after my well-being, saying: "The sufferings of the world are difficult to endure. A hundred years pass in the blink of an eye and do not wait for anyone.
Although suffering comes swiftly, virtuous conduct must take precedence; diligent study is sufficient to guide the mind. Now I shall depart to practice the Way."
Dao’an said, “To practice both is superior; if you cannot do so, then each may follow his own inclination, and I shall assist you in your joy.

[Hui]yi took it upon himself to recite five hundred thousand words of scripture and made the worship of the Buddha his primary vocation. At that time, the methods of Chan meditation had not yet been transmitted; he sat in solitary meditation according to the scriptures.
The Prince of Linchuan of the Jin dynasty treated him with great courtesy and provided him with the four requisites. Later, he stayed together with Dao’an at Taohou Temple in Chang’an. Dao’an—
After the peace was restored, during the Long’an era, he fell ill. He recited the name of Maitreya orally, never for a moment ceasing.
His disciple Zhisheng attended him during his illness and asked, "Why do you not wish to be reborn in the Western Paradise, but instead call upon Maitreya exclusively?
He replied, "We eight disciples, including Dao’an, previously made a vow to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to behold Maitreya face-to-face. Our vows have all been fulfilled first."
"I alone remain; I wish to fulfill my original vow. Having finished speaking, light immediately shone upon his body and his countenance became even more serene.
Shortly thereafter, he passed away at the age of seventy. He was buried to the right of Dao’an’s tomb (and so forth).
Zhu Fachu was a man of unknown origins. He resided at Xianyi Temple in Shanyin, Kuaiji, where he practiced asceticism with great diligence and directed his mind toward emptiness and stillness;

the community held him in high esteem. They requested that he serve as the temple’s abbot. During the Yuanxing era of the Jin dynasty, while he was supervising the repair of the temple walls, he went to Lanxiang to purchase timber from an old house.
As evening fell, he was together with the boatman who had transported the wood and the mistress of the house.

They entered the lake. In a moment, the wind arose and clouds and mist filled the four quarters. She thought to herself, "I am destined to perish here together with this woman; it would indeed be a source of shame.

Suddenly, sleet and snow fell in rapid torrents, and the surging waves rushed forward. The boat was small and water began to enter. She returned to her devotion, calling upon Avalokiteśvara and reciting the sutra.
In an instant, an empty boat appeared in the middle of the lake, coming across swiftly as if flying, until it reached the side of their vessel. She continued her recitation.

His devotion was even more profound. After a short while, he went to the place where Chun was staying to seek him out specifically, but the boat had already departed with no one on board. That the vessel was moved by such sincerity was indeed like this (and so forth).

Zhu Huqing was a native of Guangling; his mind was pure and his aspirations lofty, his discernment and contemplation were vast and far-reaching, and he did not cultivate worldly etiquette, devoting himself solely to...

He was earnest in his observance of the precepts and was gentle, benevolent, pure, and simple by nature. He possessed a refined character and virtue; he ate vegetarian food and soft herbs at all times, treating both the young and the old with equal consistency.

He delved into the study of the sutras and vinaya, and extensively researched meditation and recitation. He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Viśeṣacinti-brahma-paripṛcchā*.

Although he did not occupy the seat of honor as a Dharma Master, his understanding of the principles was concise and profound. During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he traveled to Chang’an, where he fully mastered the Way and its arts.

During the Yuanxi era of the Song dynasty, Huiqing again entered Mount Lu to seek out virtuous masters. At that time, there was a great flood in Jingzhou and Yangzhou; the waters of Xiangyang surged and overflowed in vast waves.
Just as Huiqing was about to reach Xiao Lei, a wind of auspicious appearance arrived from all sides. His companions, exerting their strength, had already entered the harbor first.
Huiqing’s boat was slow and heavy, and he had not yet caught up. Lord Yang became enraged, and towering waves rose to touch the heavens. Huiqing’s lifelong plans were at an end, and he made this vow:
He looked only toward the Buddha and recited the name of Avalokiteśvara with a mind directed nowhere else.
Those on the shore saw his boat cutting through the waves against the wind, appearing as if it were being pulled by human hands. In a mere moment, he reached the shore in safety.

Thereupon, he scattered offerings of *naivāra* and purified his heart within the realm of clarity. In every place where he traveled, he propagated the Way, [teaching] the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.

His disciples, numbering tens of thousands from both the noble and the humble, raised their voices in unison like grass bending before the wind. He extensively composed sutras and scriptures and repeatedly organized the collection of the Dharma.
At the age of sixty-two, he passed away in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuandi era (392 CE). [And so forth.]
Huiguo was a native of Yuzhou. From his childhood, he maintained pure discipline and sought the Way; he was filial toward his parents and reverent toward his teachers.

As his family was poor and lacked sufficient food and clothing, in the fourth year of the Yuanxi era, he took up his book-cases and traveled south to the capital, where he resided in a meditation cell at Waguan Temple.

Although his meals were often empty and meager, he abstained from fish and meat. He was exceptionally diligent in burning incense, performing prostrations and repentance rituals, and reciting the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
Sengguo had thoroughly studied the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Triyāna*, and the *Vaipulya* scriptures. His pure reputation and outstanding fame were equal to those of Sengju.
Once, while at Qing’s residence, Guo suddenly saw a man wearing a formal robe and cap, who bowed with palms joined in respect. Guo asked, "Who are you?
He replied, "Formerly, I was a śramaṇa of this monastery; now, as retribution, I am a ghost that eats excrement. Guo said:

[The monk] asked, "What was your name in the past? Why do you now wear this *qia* (a head covering)? He replied, “My name is not worth mentioning. When I was about to leave the monastery, I encountered an incident and returned to lay life.

[The monk] asked again, “For what transgression did you become such a ghost? He replied, “In the past, when serving as the *zhíyuè* (the monk on duty), I frequently requested food and drink, and I gave away the sauce and vinegar to beggars.
Your Virtuous Master’s moral character is revered by both the hidden and the manifest; I request that you perform a meritorious act on my behalf so that I may be released from this state.”

The monk Guo said, "You should perform prostrations and recitations. Is there anything belonging to you? He replied, "In the past, I had three thousand coins which I buried beneath a large persimmon tree in front of the eastern room.
When I left, I did not take them. I pray that you may take them for the sake of merit. Having spoken these words, he vanished.
Guo told the assembly to dig it up, and they found the three thousand coins. With this, they commissioned a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra* and used the remaining goods to host a religious assembly.
More than a month after the assembly, he dreamed of this ghost, who said of itself: "I am due to be reborn; therefore, I have not yet been able to report my great recovery here.
Indeed, when benevolence and love reach far and wide, serving as a bridge for the world, it is always like this.
At seventy-six years of age, he passed away in the sixth year of the Taishi era (etc.).
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Twenty-four:

Daohai of Jiangling was a man of rigorous conduct and diligent cultivation. From his youth until his maturity, he maintained a consistent standard; he lived in poverty and observed frugal restraint, never altering his principles.
Once, at Changsha Temple, as the winter *zhai* (fasting retreat) was about to conclude, the monks there collectively performed the *zhai* for Amitābha.
Haisu was empty-handed and possessed nothing to offer to the assembly. He then roused his resolve with renewed vigor and burned two fingers as an offering;

he subsequently engaged in intensive questioning until he nearly collapsed from exhaustion. At that time, the various masters and monks said to him, "Simply take refuge in Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."
He was able to recover from his pain. Thereupon, he forged his mind with right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), and in an instant he was healed.
Later, at dusk, he went out from beneath the stupa to perform walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). Consequently, he became critically ill. When evening approached on the following day, he said:

"Today there is a superior person in the air who comes from afar to welcome me. Yet my residence is still lowly and humble; this must be because my meritorious karma has not yet accumulated. Thus he spoke clearly.
Regarding retribution, he exhorted them on the merit [of practice]. Having finished speaking, he lay down peacefully and passed away with a serene expression (and so forth).
Daofa’s original surname was Cao; he was a native of Dunhuang. His meditative contemplation transcended that of ordinary men, and his ascetic practices illuminated the three miserable realms.
Hearing that the region of Shu was somewhat inclined toward faith, he traveled there through the mountain passes at the request of Wang Xiuzhen and Fei Keng.

He served as the abbot of both Xingle and Xiangji Monasteries. When begging for alms to provide offerings for the midday meal, he would regularly set aside his own portion to give to insects and birds.

He practiced seated meditation and recited scriptures day and night without negligence. Every evening, he would strip off his robes and place them before an image of Maitreya to feed the mosquitoes and gadflies.
He continued this for many years, after which he beheld Maitreya emitting various kinds of light; from the center of these, a white light shone straight upward.
He entered hell and beheld his former associates as well as all sentient beings undergoing suffering. Furthermore, regarding the *Shanshenzhou* (Spirits-Goodness Dhāraṇī):
in the second year of the Yuánhuí era, while engaged in meditative contemplation, he passed away upon his meditation couch (*shéngchuáng*)... [and so forth].
Sengye’s original surname was Feng; he was a native of Chengdu in Shu Commandery. He was a man of austere conduct who strictly observed the Vinaya precepts.

He maintained a vegetarian diet with great vigor, such that his mind and body were never bound by worldly attachments. Qian Sheng, the Governor of Jiyang in Dangqu, had served the non-Buddhist teachings throughout his life.
Suddenly, he dreamed that he entered a temple to pay his respects and saw a white jade bead, four inches long, suspended in mid-air. Furthermore, there were scattered robes, rising high...
He covered it with them. Furthermore, there was another layer of pearls that followed his hand. At dawn, he encountered the monk Sengye and recounted his dream together.

Sengye then encouraged and inspired him, whereupon he was able to apply himself with diligence. Together they purchased land, and in the fifth year of the Yuanhui era, they established a monastery there.
It was called the Maitreya Temple, named after what he had realized. He then moved his residence there; loathing his defiled physical form, he aspired for that eternal bliss (and so forth).
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Twenty-five: Fahui.

His original surname was Li, and he was a native of Gaochang. In his youth, he delighted in hunting and archery, and was addicted to wine and stringed music. His wife was so beautiful that she was peerless in the entire country;
sons of wealthy and noble families vied with one another to have illicit relations with her. One day, as Fahui was out on an excursion, he encountered a powerful man...
Fù struck him. His friend informed him of this. Huì reflected to himself: "I possess great strength; he will surely kill me.
He fled to Kucha and wished to leave the household life. Being poor, he had no monastic robes. When foreigners die there, they clothe the corpse in fine garments and send it to the Śītavana cemetery.
Huì took his leave and returned, following another funeral procession until the family left him behind. There, he stripped the clothing from a dead person and encountered [a monk].

A *vetāla* (corpse-raising spirit) arose; it repeatedly shifted its position up and down for seven turns. Huìshuài emerged victorious, stripping the spirit of its garments and selling them for three thousand coins, which he used to procure dharma robes.
He subsequently left the household life to cultivate meditation and discipline. His ascetic practices were peerless;
he subsisted on simple vegetarian food and skillfully guided others with a mind free from judgment of right or wrong. Later, he returned to Gaochang and resided at Xiankui Monastery. His virtue...

As Sengxiao had already passed away, the community of nuns relied upon him for guidance and received his sincere instruction. Only the nun Feng of Jindu Langzhong Temple often said to Huì, "Ācārya, you are not yet well-established;
you should go to the kingdom of Kucha. During the period when she was serving as the month-steward (zhíyuè) under the commandant of Jinhua Temple, she continued to urge him.
She was to obtain the supreme Dharma. Huisi sent a nun to Kucha with this message. Upon arriving, she saw the monk on duty (zhíyuè), who was delighted.
He invited her into his room and gave her one dou five sheng of grape wine, ordering her to drink it. Huisi was greatly shocked and amazed.

I have been pure for a long time; originally seeking the Dharma, I instead drank the medicine of non-Dharma. Though I stubbornly clung to it and refused to leave, the duty officer urgently pushed me out.
Hui then withdrew to reflect and did not dare disobey; having disobeyed, I suddenly drank it all at once. Intoxicated, I asked questions and then lay down.
The duty officer locked the room and went on to other duties. When Hui awoke from the wine, he felt deep remorse and thought: "I have suddenly committed an offense."
He observed the precepts, repented and reproached himself, and beat his body, intending to take his own life. Within this brief period, he attained the third fruit [of Arhatship].

When the monk on duty returned and questioned him, he replied, "I have attained it. Later, he returned to Gaochang, where he widely propagated the Sūtras and Vinaya; both monastics and laypeople turned to him with reverence.

Huiqin’s reputation spread throughout the local districts. In the first year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away while sitting upright without illness, with his fingers curled into the shape of the number four, as recorded by his disciple Huizhao.
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Twenty-six:
Sengbiao. His original surname was Gao, and he was a native of Liangzhou. He possessed courageous and vigorous resolve.

Having heard that the Buddha’s almsbowl was in the country of Bolor—that bowl is currently at the Tai Temple in Jibin—and that five hundred arhats constantly made offerings to it, the bowl passed through Teng...

He traveled by air to the Cool Continent (Sītādvīpa), where twelve arhats were staying according to the resting of their alms bowls. Six years later, he returned to Kaśmīra. The monastic community expressed regret that they had not been able to see him.
He then traveled westward across the Pamir Mountains, wishing to pay his sincere respects; he also intended to go to the kingdom of Yutian (Khotan). However, the road to Kaśmīra was blocked.
In Yutian, the king sent a letter along with a replica of the Buddha’s bowl, which Zhang Zhi wrote for him, and presented it to him. Furthermore, he asked:
"Is there anything further you wish for? He replied, "I have heard it said that the image of the Victorious One made by Māgha is most similar to the true likeness of the Buddha;

I wish to obtain it for veneration. The King immediately commissioned skilled artisans to fashion a gilded gold image, one zhang in height and breadth, and placed authentic śarīra relics within its crown. The monk Biao then escorted it back to Liangzhou. Thus it is known.
As the land of Liang was about to fall, he intended to return to Huaihai. Passing through Xingping County in Shu, the śramaṇa Daowang requested that he halt there to pay homage to the bowl and image.
These are now at Longhua Temple there; the monk Biao entered it and paid reverence to the stone image, remaining for two years.
He passed away at the monastery (as detailed above).

Zhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou. He possessed refined talent and character, and his religious practice was diligent and sincere. Clad in coarse cloth and subsisting on vegetarian fare, he practiced extensive charity and compassion.
It is further suspected that during his childhood, he had once received the five precepts; having perhaps committed some transgression against them, he later received full ordination.
He was concerned that he might not have received the precepts. Having practiced meditative contemplation for many years, he could not resolve the matter himself and suffered great distress.
He then traveled again by sea with his disciples Zhìyǔ and Zhídá to India to consult an arhat regarding this matter.

The arhat was likewise unable to decide it, so he entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and went to Tuṣita Heaven to ask Maitreya. Maitreya replied that he had indeed received the precepts. Yán [was thus reassured].
Filled with great joy, he then returned on foot to Jibin, where he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-eight.
His disciples, Zhìyǔ and Zhìdá, returned and transmitted these words (as detailed above).

Baoyun was a native of Hebei. His character was circumscribed yet simple and upright, earning him the praise of his teachers and friends. In the fourteenth year of the Taiyuan era, at the age of eighteen, he entered Mount Lu.
At that time, the construction of the Prajñā Terrace had begun; with few monks available to oversee the work, Baoyun personally supervised the laying of stones and the piling of earth.
Yun threw a stone, and as the stones struck one another, it happened by mistake that a calf was hit and killed. He was filled with shame, resentment, and despondency for many years.
In the first year of the Long’an era, he took his leave to enter the Western Regions, vowing to visit all sacred sites and personally perform repentance.
He then traveled to Khotan and various kingdoms of India. His departure together with Zhiyan and Faxian was the same, yet their subsequent journeys differed.
In the kingdom of Tāla, he beheld a golden-leafed Maitreya Buddha image, eight *zhang* in height.
He prostrated himself beneath the statue and offered sincere repentance for fifty days. At night, he saw a divine light shining brilliantly, as bright as the break of dawn. He gazed [upon it].
They filled the roads. Those venerable śramaṇas of long-standing virtue all remarked that such numinous radiance was frequently seen (and so forth).
Fasheng’s original surname was Li; he was a native of Longxi who resided in Gaochang. He left home to become a monk at the age of nine and applied himself diligently to recitation and study.
Every day he would say: "I have not yet established the three firm foundations; the five aggregates arise and perish, and all unions end in separation—all this is due to delusion and craving.

If one does not sever the three poisons, how can one seek liberation? At the age of nineteen, he encountered the śramaṇa Zhimeng, who had returned from foreign lands and recounted various miraculous accounts.
Thereupon, [Daorong] conceived a resolute aspiration. He took leave of his parents and led a group of teachers and friends, numbering twenty-nine people.
He traveled far to India, passing through various kingdoms in search of sacred relics and auspicious signs, prostrating and making offerings to express his devotion through the three karmas.

To the northeast of the kingdom of Changyou, he beheld a statue of Maitreya made of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood, eight *xun* in height—one *xun* being equivalent to one *zhang* of this country. This was during the four hundred and eighty years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
There was an Arhat named Kālika Nanda who, for the sake of saving sentient beings, ascended to Tuṣita Heaven and transcribed the true form of the Buddha;
he then sealed this image, which constantly emits radiance. The fourfold assembly provides music and rejoices in laughter throughout the four seasons.

People from afar all come to repent before the image, and there are none whose vows fail to be fulfilled; they attain the first fruit of the Path by the dozens each year, and [the fame of] this place spreads widely to all quarters.
Five hundred people, both monastics and laypeople, vowed to sacrifice their bodies so that they might surely behold Maitreya; this aspiration was to be fulfilled.
The incense smoke curled to the right, and in an instant, the various clouds of smoke merged into a single canopy, rotating three times to the right before gradually fading away (and so forth).
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume Twenty-seven: Senggong was a native of Yuzhou.
From his youth, he maintained high principles and became renowned for his virtue in observing the precepts. He resided at Waguan Temple.

Later, he recruited like-minded companions to cast a sixteen-foot golden image. When the casting was first completed and the mold had not yet been removed, it was unknown whether the work would be beautiful or flawed. At that time...
In the twelfth year of the Yixi era, the prohibition against casting copper was extremely strict; those who violated it were sentenced to death.

Senggong was arrested by the authorities and brought before the administration of Xiangzhou for trial on charges of illicit conduct. His shackles and fetters were so heavy that he had no further hope of survival.

He focused his mind single-mindedly on Avalokiteśvara and recited the sutras day and night for about a month. Then, in a dream, he saw the statue he had cast arrive within the prison and stroke him with its hand.
Tou asked him, "Are you afraid? Gong replied, "I am certain that I will die. The image said, "Have no cause for worry.

Gong observed the features of the image and saw that on its chest, about a foot square, the copper-colored surface was parched and bubbling. Once the *rāva* (the ritual) was completed, it reached the day of the execution.
The military officer was to come and supervise the execution. When he mounted the carriage, the oxen refused to enter; once they had entered, they bolted, and the carriage was immediately destroyed.
Consequently, the date for the execution was set again. Then an imperial edict arrived at Pengcheng, stating that if there were monks who had not yet been executed, they might be pardoned.
He was thus successfully rescued. Upon returning, he saw that the statue he had cast indeed bore scorch marks upon its chest.
Since the offering had proven auspicious and efficacious, Qing responded with daily diligence until his death (and so forth).
Daojiao was a native of Gaolu. By nature he was pure and frugal; he maintained a vegetarian diet and devoted himself to meditation and recitation.

He resided at Longhua Temple, where he took sole responsibility for its affairs and served the visiting monks with great devotion. In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era, he dedicated his clothing and resources to inspire others toward the study of the Dharma.
Together with Zhu Chuan-sun, a resident of Jiankang, he constructed a three-bay Buddha hall, as well as various flowered banners and a *mi-le* (Maitreya) image made of layered ramie cloth.
There is one statue of the Buddha leaning against it, sixteen feet in height. Its divine countenance is dignified and solemn, inspiring faith and awakening.
He was ninety-three years old and passed away in the twenty-sixth year [of the reign] (and so forth).

Tanduo’s original surname was Zou, and he was a native of Yeyang. He was pure, upright, and possessed a distinguished reputation. Having entered the Path at the age of ten or so, he resided at Anle Temple.
Having cultivated the causes for his awakening in previous lives, his assets were abundant and accumulated; yet, although he possessed gold in abundance, he did not allow it to burden his mind.

He practiced compassion, knew contentment, and always harbored a sense of empathy and sorrow within him, making the salvation of sentient beings his primary concern. He served as an attendant to the śramaṇa Baozhi.
He was highly revered. He often remarked, "This person is a companion on the path to the five dharmas.

Every time he mentioned this, he would say, "You shall be born in Tuṣita and diligently serve Maitreya," thus fulfilling his original vow and acceding to his long-held aspiration. Thereupon, he relinquished his wealth and property to produce copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Amitāyus-sūtra*, the *Maitreya-sūtra*, the *Catuḥpariṣat-sūtra*, the *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra*, the names of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, and the *Prātimokṣa* for monks and nuns, respectively.

He produced one thousand copies [of the scriptures]. He fashioned one hundred thousand *poṣadha* counting-slips (*śalākā*) and disseminated them to distant regions, spreading his transformative influence across foreign lands.

He elucidated the subtle and profound, exhausting his wealth to propagate the Teaching and exhausting his thoughts on its deep mysteries. His responses were as swift as reaching for a door, and his observance of the precepts was refined and lofty.

Being solely devoted and diligent, he even attained communication through dreams. Someone said to him: "If your karma for Tuṣita Heaven has already been accomplished, there is nothing further to be done."
Furthermore, he had visions. He also dreamed that Maitreya Buddha stroked his crown with his hand; divine fragrances, banners, and the presence of spirit-dragons manifested upon his body.
For one or two years, such miraculous responses occurred continuously. At over sixty years of age, in the fourth year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty, he passed away.
Zhou Yangrenyi, the Commandant of Wuling and younger brother of Zhizhi, erected this stele (as recorded).
Biographies of Eminent Monks, Volume 28:
Shi Faxiang was diligent and possessed high moral integrity. In the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, he established the Maitreya Vihāra (and so forth).
On the final day of the fifth month in the second year of the Mun-ryeol era (at the hour of the horse), this was completed at the Southern Hall of Fukujō-in in Kasagi-ji Temple.

Having secluded myself on the mountain from the thirteenth day of the same month, I have extracted these essential passages concerning Maitreya’s spiritual responses from among the thirty volumes of the *Ming seng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks). Apart from these, there are other most vital accounts.
This commentary is merely recorded here for the time being and set aside. This book has circulated throughout the world;

I only hope that from time to time, someone will conceive a diligent and great vow to transcribe this essential text of Maitreya. Although it may seem like a trivial matter, it is solely for the sake of providing for future reference.
Those within the monastic lineage should take pity on this intention. I look up to you and pray that you will preserve these essential passages found in various places.
The merit of transcribing this excerpted text shall surely result in the karmic connection of being constantly accompanied by Maitreya throughout successive lifetimes.
Written by the temple resident monk Sōshō, who placed his writing-brush and straw hat [here].
(Appendix) First Account of the Transmission of Famous Monks Regarding the Sarvāstivāda School,
compiled by Sengyou from the *Chusanzang jiji*.
The account of Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna;
the account of Senghui’s three-week prayer and the resulting response of the śarīra;
and how the majestic power of the śarīra is not merely luminous, for even the fires that consume the kalpa cannot burn it, as it is adamantine.
The pestle could not destroy the matter;
it was only when Kumārajīva saw the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra* that he first understood the matters of the Mahāyāna.
In a dream, Śākyamuni Tathāgata stroked Kumārajīva’s head with his hand and said, "Arise! If you have thoughts of desire, repent immediately.
Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master, then translated thirty-eight works comprising two hundred and ninety fascicles, including the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other sūtras and śāstras.
In the fourth fascicle, regarding the affairs of the Han lands, three thousand disciples followed Kumārajīva in his dharma activities.
As Kumārajīva was approaching death, the assembly of monks took their leave of him, saying: "The Affairs."
The Third Account: How Kumārajīva’s Tongue Remained Intact After His Cremation,
Concerning the Matter of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* Not Being Available in the Land of Song.
The original name of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain was Vyāghrīpura;
it has been twenty years since [the Buddha] received full ordination; there are differing accounts regarding these matters between the Western lands and this land;
